terms.def: Nonliving: the physical and chemical parts of an ecosystem, such as temperature, sunlight, water, minerals and wind.

Acids that fall from the air in rain, snow or fog (wet deposition) or as dry particles and gases (dry deposition). It forms when sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react in the air to make sulfuric and nitric acid. Often called acid rain.

Acidic water that flows from mines and mine waste. Sulfide minerals exposed to air and water form sulfuric acid, which lowers the pH of streams and dissolves toxic metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic from the rock.
Solar systems that use equipment such as pumps, fans or mirrors to collect and move the sun's heat, including rooftop water heaters and concentrated solar power plants.

Acute exposure is short, often a single high dose, with effects soon after (an acute effect). Chronic exposure is long or repeated, often at low doses, with effects that may take months or years to appear (a chronic effect).

A heritable trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment, such as thick fur in a cold climate. Adaptations become common in a population through natural selection over many generations, not within one organism’s lifetime.

A graph of how many people (or what percent of a population) are in each age group, usually with males on the left and females on the right and the youngest at the bottom. Also called a population pyramid. Its shape predicts whether a population will grow, stay stable or shrink.
The share of incoming sunlight a surface reflects. Snow and ice have a high albedo; open ocean and forest have a low albedo and absorb more energy.

A rapid increase in algae in water, often fed by extra nutrients. Blooms turn water green, block sunlight, and when they die their decomposition uses up dissolved oxygen. Some, called harmful algal blooms, release toxins.
The release of ammonium into the soil by decomposers as they break down nitrogen in wastes and dead organisms.
NH4+, a form of nitrogen made by nitrogen fixation and ammonification. Plants can take it up, and its positive charge helps soil particles hold it. Ammonia (NH3) is the related gas.
A predator at the top of its feeding sequence, with no natural predators as an adult, such as a wolf, orca or eagle.
Raising fish, shellfish or water plants in controlled conditions, such as ponds, tanks or net pens in the sea, for food. It now supplies about half of the fish and shellfish people eat.
An underground layer of porous rock or sediment, such as sand, gravel or sandstone, that holds groundwater and lets it flow to wells.

The drawing down of groundwater when it is pumped out faster than rain and snowmelt refill (recharge) the aquifer. Around a pumping well the water table drops in a funnel shape called a cone of depression; nearby shallow wells can go dry.
A fibrous mineral once used in insulation, tiles and pipe wrap. When it is damaged, its fibers get into the air and can cause lung disease and cancer if breathed in.
The uptake of nitrate or ammonium by plant roots and its use to build proteins and DNA; animals assimilate nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
The tilt of Earth's axis, about 23.5°, which keeps pointing the same way as Earth orbits the Sun. It causes the seasons: the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun has summer.
A baghouse filter: a set of large fabric bags that smokestack gas is forced through, trapping particles the way a vacuum cleaner bag does.
The build-up of a substance in one organism over its lifetime, because it is taken in faster than it is broken down or excreted. Persistent, fat-soluble substances bioaccumulate.
The variety of life in an area, measured at three levels: genetic diversity within populations, species diversity within communities, and habitat diversity within an area.
A liquid or gas fuel made from biomass, such as ethanol fermented from corn or sugarcane, biodiesel from plant oils or animal fats, and biogas from manure or waste.
Biological control: using a pest's natural enemies, such as predators (ladybugs, lacewings), parasitic wasps or disease organisms, to keep the pest's population down.
The increase in concentration of a persistent, fat-soluble substance at each higher trophic level of a food chain, so top predators carry the highest levels.
The total mass of living (or recently living) organisms in an area, often measured as dry mass in grams per square meter.
A large region of the Earth with a typical climate and typical plants and animals, such as tundra, desert or tropical rainforest. The same biome can occur on several continents.
Living, or once living: the organisms of an ecosystem and the dead matter they leave. Plants, animals, fungi and bacteria are biotic factors.

The fastest rate at which a population could grow if it had unlimited resources and no limits. It depends on how many offspring each individual produces, how early it starts and how often it reproduces.
Buffering capacity: the ability of soil, rock or water to neutralize acid and resist a change in pH. Limestone gives lakes and soils a high buffering capacity; granite gives little.
Animals caught by fishing gear that were not the target of the catch, such as dolphins, sea turtles, sharks, seabirds and young fish. Much bycatch dies and is thrown back.

The movement of carbon among the atmosphere, living things, soil, the ocean, sediments and rock, and fossil fuels, by processes such as photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion and sedimentation.
CO2, a gas made of one carbon and two oxygen atoms. It is taken in by photosynthesis and released by respiration, decomposition and combustion.

The total amount of carbon dioxide (and other heat-trapping gases, counted as carbon dioxide) released by a person, product or activity, usually in metric tons of carbon dioxide per year. It counts emissions only, so it is one part of an ecological footprint.
CO, a colorless, odorless gas from incomplete burning of fuel. It binds to hemoglobin in the blood and reduces the oxygen the blood can carry.
A reservoir that takes in more carbon than it releases, such as a growing forest or the ocean. A carbon source releases more carbon than it takes in.

Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) forms when CO₂ dissolves in water and releases hydrogen ions. Those ions bind carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻), leaving less for organisms to build calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) shells and skeletons.
The largest population of a species that an environment can support over time with its food, water, space and other resources. Written K. It can change when the environment changes.
A device in a vehicle's exhaust system that uses metal catalysts to change carbon monoxide into CO2, nitrogen oxides into nitrogen gas, and unburned hydrocarbons into CO2 and water.
The process in which living things break down sugar with oxygen to release energy, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
A shrubland biome with hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters, where shrubs with small waxy leaves grow and fires are common.

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs): stable, nontoxic gases of chlorine, fluorine and carbon once used as refrigerants, propellants in spray cans and in foams. In the stratosphere, UV breaks them and frees chlorine that destroys ozone.

The main United States law on air pollution (1970, with later amendments). It lets the EPA set air quality standards for the criteria pollutants and limit what cars, power plants and factories release.

A logging method that cuts down all or nearly all of the trees in an area at once. It is the cheapest and fastest way to harvest timber, but it exposes soil to erosion, warms nearby streams and removes habitat.

A long-term change in Earth’s climate. Global climate change today means warming caused mainly by greenhouse gases from human activity, and its effects on sea level, weather and ecosystems (global warming is the temperature part).
A graph of a place’s average temperature and precipitation for each month of the year, used to identify its biome.
The mature, relatively stable community that develops at the end of succession if there is no major disruption for a long time, such as an old forest. Also called a mature community.

A solid fossil fuel formed from plants buried in swamps and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years; it ranks from lignite to bituminous to anthracite as its carbon and energy content rise.
Combined heat and power: using the waste heat from making electricity to heat buildings or water, so more of the fuel's energy is put to use.
A group of people born during the same span of years, shown as one bar of an age structure diagram, such as everyone aged 0 to 9.
Burning: a fuel reacts with oxygen and releases energy, carbon dioxide and water. Burning fossil fuels or wood moves stored carbon into the atmosphere.
A relationship in which one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed (+/0).
All the populations of different species that live and interact in the same area.
An interaction in which organisms use the same limited resource, so each gets less and both are harmed. It can be between species or within one species.
Letting microbes break down food scraps, yard waste and paper with oxygen to make humus-rich compost for soil. It keeps organic waste out of landfills, where it would make methane.

A concentrated animal feeding operation (feedlot): a facility that keeps large numbers of animals, such as cattle, hogs or chickens, in a small space and brings feed to them. It produces meat cheaply on little land, but concentrates manure, uses antibiotics heavily, and depends on grain grown elsewhere.
The change of water vapor into liquid droplets as air cools, which forms clouds, fog and dew.
An organism that gets energy by eating other organisms (a heterotroph). Primary consumers eat producers, secondary consumers eat primary consumers, and tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
Plowing and planting in rows that follow the contour lines of a slope (across it) rather than running up and down it. Each row acts as a small dam that slows runoff and catches soil.
A loop of motion in a fluid heated from below: warm, less dense material rises, spreads, cools and sinks. Convection currents in Earth's mantle move the tectonic plates.

A plate boundary where two plates move toward each other. A denser ocean plate sinks under the other plate (subduction), forming a trench, earthquakes and volcanoes; two continents crumple into high mountains.
A fraction whose top and bottom are equal amounts in different units, such as 1 kWh / 3,412 BTU or 3.79 L / 1 gal, so multiplying by it does not change the amount.
The whitening of corals when stress, usually warm water, makes them expel the algae that live in their tissues and feed them. Without the algae, corals may starve and die.
A structure built by colonies of coral animals in warm, clear, shallow seawater. Algae living inside the coral share food from photosynthesis in a mutualism.
The deflection of moving air or water caused by Earth's rotation: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
One of six common air pollutants the EPA sets national limits for under the Clean Air Act: carbon monoxide, lead, nitrogen dioxide, ozone, particulate matter and sulfur dioxide.

Growing different crops in a field in a planned order from year to year, for example corn, then soybeans, then wheat. It breaks pest and disease cycles and, when a legume is included, adds nitrogen to the soil.
The number of live births in a year for every 1,000 people in a population. Written CBR.
The number of deaths in a year for every 1,000 people in a population. Written CDR.
An ecosystem service that provides nonmaterial benefits: recreation, tourism, beauty, spiritual value and opportunities for education and research.

DDT: a persistent insecticide widely used from the 1940s, banned for most uses in the United States in 1972. It caused thin eggshells in birds of prey. PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls) are persistent industrial chemicals once used in electrical equipment.
The unit (dB) for sound level. The scale is logarithmic: each increase of 10 dB is 10 times the sound intensity. Long exposure at or above about 85 dB can damage hearing.
An organism, mostly bacteria and fungi, that breaks down dead matter and wastes, returning nutrients to the soil and carbon to the air.
The breakdown of dead matter and wastes by decomposers, which releases carbon dioxide (or methane where oxygen is scarce) and returns nutrients to the soil.

The removal of a forest, or a large part of one, so the land is no longer forest, often to make room for farms, pasture, mines or cities. It releases stored carbon as carbon dioxide and removes habitat.

A model of how a country’s crude birth and death rates change as it develops economically: both start high, the death rate falls first, then the birth rate falls, and both end low. It has four stages.
The conversion by bacteria in low-oxygen soil or water of nitrate back into N2 gas, which returns to the atmosphere.
A limiting factor whose effect grows stronger as a population becomes denser, such as food shortage, competition, disease or predation.
A limiting factor that affects a population whatever its size or density, such as a flood, a frost, a fire or a drought.
A renewable resource that can run down if it is used faster than it is replaced, such as wood cut faster than the forest regrows.
A biome that gets very little precipitation (usually under 25 cm a year), with plants that store water; it can be hot or cold.

The degradation of land in dry regions into land that behaves like a desert: lost plant cover, eroded and dried-out soil, and much lower productivity. Overgrazing, deforestation, poor farming and drought all contribute.
An organism, such as an earthworm, millipede or crab, that eats detritus (dead organic matter) and breaks it into smaller pieces, speeding decomposition.

A developed country has a high average income, widespread schooling and health care, and usually slow population growth; a developing country has a lower average income and usually a younger, faster-growing population.
A sharp drop in a population after overshoot, as individuals starve, sicken or fail to reproduce because resources have run short. Also called a population crash.
A method of converting units by multiplying by conversion factors arranged so that unwanted units cancel, leaving only the units of the answer. Also called the factor-label method.
A living thing, often an insect such as a mosquito or flea, that carries a pathogen from one host to another. A vector-borne disease spreads this way.
Oxygen gas dissolved in water, in mg/L, which fish and other aquatic animals use. Cold, moving water holds more of it than warm, still water.
A plate boundary where two plates move apart. Magma rises and forms new crust, building mid-ocean ridges (seafloor spreading) or rift valleys on land.
The amount of a substance that enters an organism, usually given in milligrams per kilogram of body mass (mg/kg) so animals of different sizes can be compared.
A graph of the percent of a test population responding (for example, dying) against the dose. It is usually S-shaped and is used to read the threshold dose, the LD50 and the ED50.
The time a quantity growing at a steady percent rate takes to double, about 70 divided by the percent growth rate.
terms.topicTitle: Growth Rates, Doubling Time and the Rule of 70

terms.def: Irrigation that delivers water slowly through tubes with small holes placed at the base of each plant. It is the most efficient method (only about 5% of the water is lost, so about 95% reaches the roots) but the most expensive to install.
Discarded electronics such as phones, computers and televisions. They contain toxic metals such as lead, mercury and cadmium as well as valuable metals, so they need special recycling or disposal.

The area of biologically productive land and water needed to supply the resources a person or population uses (food, wood, fibers, space for buildings) and to absorb its carbon dioxide waste. It is often given in global hectares per person and compared with the biocapacity available.
The gradual change in the species that make up a community after a disruption, in a series of stages that usually leads toward a mature, more stable community.
All the living things in an area together with the nonliving parts (water, soil, light, air) and the ways they interact.

A benefit that people receive from a working ecosystem, such as clean water, food, pollination or recreation. Ecosystem services are grouped into four kinds: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting.
Effective dose 50%: the dose that causes a chosen nonlethal effect, such as illness or sleep, in half of a test population.
The share of energy put in that comes out in a useful form: useful output ÷ input × 100. Ecological efficiency is the share of energy passed from one trophic level to the next, about 10%.

The warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO): the trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east across the Pacific, upwelling off South America weakens and rain shifts east. It recurs every 2 to 7 years.
A device that removes particles from smokestack gas by giving them an electric charge and collecting them on plates with the opposite charge.
A species in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant part of its range. A threatened species is one likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future.

The Endangered Species Act (US, 1973) lists threatened and endangered species, bans harming them and protects their critical habitat. CITES, an international treaty, controls trade in protected species and their parts.
A chemical that interferes with the body's hormones by mimicking them, blocking their receptors, or changing how much is made. Examples include atrazine, BPA, phthalates and synthetic estrogens.
Using less energy, usually by changing behavior, such as turning off lights, lowering the thermostat or driving less.
The amount of energy a person, country or the world uses in a period, given as a total (such as exajoules per year) or per person (such as gigajoules per person per year).
Getting the same service with less energy, such as LED bulbs, insulation or appliances and cars that use less energy for the same work.

A diagram of the energy at each trophic level, which always narrows going up because energy is lost as heat at each step. A biomass pyramid shows mass and a pyramid of numbers shows counts of organisms.

A measurement that shows the condition of an environment and how it is changing, such as biodiversity, food production, atmospheric carbon dioxide and temperature, human population, and the remaining supply of resources. Indicators show whether a system is moving toward or away from sustainability.
The removal and transport of soil or rock by wind, water or ice. It speeds up where plants are removed and the ground is left bare.
The area where a river meets the sea and fresh and salt water mix. Rich in nutrients and sunlight, estuaries are nurseries for many fish and shellfish.

The enrichment of a body of water with nutrients, especially nitrogen and phosphorus, which leads to excess algae growth. Cultural eutrophication is the rapid kind caused by human sources such as fertilizer and sewage. An oligotrophic lake is low in nutrients; a eutrophic one is high.
The change of liquid water into water vapor, powered by the sun’s energy; most of it happens at the ocean surface.
Growth by a constant percent each period, so the number added gets larger each time. It happens when resources are unlimited and gives a J-shaped curve (J-curve).
A substance added to soil to supply nutrients, mainly nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, so plants grow more.

The laws of energy. The first law: energy is not created or destroyed, only changed in form. The second law: each energy transfer turns some energy into heat that is less useful, so no transfer is 100% efficient.

The drop of a fish stock to a small fraction of its former size, so that catches fall sharply and fishing for it is no longer worthwhile. A collapsed stock may take decades to recover, or may not recover.

Irrigation that covers a whole field with a sheet of water, as in many rice paddies. It is the cheapest method, but much of the water can evaporate, run off or soak below the roots, and it can waterlog the soil.
The movement of a substance from one reservoir to another, often given as an amount per year.
A single sequence of organisms, each eaten by the next, showing one path that energy and matter take from producers to top consumers.
All the interconnected food chains in an ecosystem, showing that most organisms eat and are eaten by several species.
A VOC given off by pressed-wood furniture, cabinets, glues and some fabrics, especially when new. It irritates the eyes, nose and throat and can cause cancer.
Coal, oil or natural gas: the remains of ancient organisms buried and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years. They store carbon from the slow part of the carbon cycle.
An aquatic biome with very low salinity: lakes, ponds, rivers, streams and freshwater wetlands.
Irrigation in which water flows down shallow trenches (furrows) dug between crop rows. It is cheap and simple, but a large share of the water evaporates or runs off the end of the field.

A species with a broad niche: it eats many kinds of food, lives in many habitats and tolerates a wide range of conditions, such as raccoons and coyotes. Generalists cope well with environmental change.

The variety of genes (and so of heritable traits) among the individuals of one population or species. High genetic diversity makes it more likely that some individuals survive a new disease or a change in conditions.

A genetically modified organism: a plant, animal or microbe whose DNA has been changed in a laboratory, for example by adding a gene from another species, to give it a new trait such as resistance to an insect pest.
Heat from Earth's interior, from radioactive decay and heat left from Earth's formation, used to make electricity where hot rock is near the surface or to heat buildings.
Global warming potential (GWP): how much heat a mass of a gas traps over a set time, usually 100 years, compared with the same mass of carbon dioxide (GWP 1). Mass × GWP gives the CO₂ equivalent.

The rapid rise in crop yields from about the 1940s to the 1970s, first in Mexico and then in South Asia and beyond, from high-yield grain varieties grown with synthetic fertilizer, irrigation, pesticides and machines.

A roof covered with soil and plants. It soaks up rain and releases it slowly, cools the building and the air around it, and gives habitat to insects and birds; it costs more to build because the roof must carry the extra weight.

The warming of Earth’s surface and lower atmosphere because greenhouse gases absorb infrared from the surface and re-emit part of it downward. The natural effect keeps Earth about 33 °C warmer; added gases strengthen it.
A gas that absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation, warming the lower atmosphere: water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs and HFCs (GHGs).
Gross primary productivity: the total rate at which producers capture energy by photosynthesis, before any is used for their own respiration.
A ground source heat pump uses electricity to move heat between a building and the ground a few meters down, which stays at a steady temperature, heating in winter and cooling in summer.
Ozone (O3) in the lowest layer of the atmosphere, where people breathe. It forms when sunlight splits NO2 and the freed oxygen atom joins O2. It irritates lungs and damages plants.
Water that fills the pores and cracks in soil and rock below the surface; it moves slowly and supplies wells and springs.
How fast a quantity grows, as a percent of its size per unit of time: a growth rate of 2% a year adds 2 for every 100 each year.
terms.topicTitle: Growth Rates, Doubling Time and the Rule of 70

terms.def: The place where an organism or population lives, with the conditions it needs.
The variety of different habitats (forest, meadow, stream, wetland) in an area. More habitat diversity supports more species. Also called ecosystem diversity.

The breaking of a large, continuous habitat into smaller patches separated by roads, farms, towns or other land its species cannot use. The patches act like islands, and small, isolated patches tend to lose species.
The destruction or conversion of the places species live, by farming, logging, mining, roads and cities (habitat destruction). It is the leading cause of biodiversity loss.

Large loops of rising and sinking air in each hemisphere: the Hadley cell (equator to about 30°), the Ferrel cell (about 30° to 60°) and the polar cell (about 60° to the pole). Air rises near the equator and 60° (wet) and sinks near 30° and the poles (dry).
The time it takes for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay; amount left = starting amount × 0.5^(time ÷ half-life).
A hazy, low-visibility sky caused by tiny particles in the air that scatter and absorb sunlight. Smoke, dust and pollution particles all cause haze.
An animal that eats plants or algae (a primary consumer). A carnivore eats animals; an omnivore eats both plants and animals.
An acronym for the main human threats to biodiversity: Habitat loss, Invasive species, Pollution, human Population growth, Climate change and Overexploitation.
A place where a column of hot mantle rock stays fixed while a plate moves over it, building a chain of volcanoes that get older in the direction the plate moves, such as the Hawaiian Islands.
Dark, crumbly organic matter in soil, left when decomposers break down dead plants and animals. It holds water and slowly releases nutrients.
A vehicle that pairs a gasoline engine with an electric motor and battery, recapturing braking energy to use less fuel; an electric vehicle runs on a battery alone.
Hydraulic fracturing: pumping water, sand and chemicals under high pressure into shale rock to crack it and free natural gas or oil.

Replacements for CFCs. Hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) still contain some chlorine, so they deplete a little ozone and are being phased out. Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) contain no chlorine and spare ozone, but many trap heat strongly and are being phased down under the 2016 Kigali Amendment.
Electricity made by water falling through a turbine that turns a generator, usually at a dam that holds water in a reservoir.
A hydrogen fuel cell combines hydrogen and oxygen chemically, without burning, to make electricity; its only exhaust is water, but the hydrogen must first be made using energy.
The water cycle: the movement of water among the ocean, atmosphere, land, ice, living things and groundwater by evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration.
A state of very low dissolved oxygen in water, below what most fish and bottom animals need. Large hypoxic areas are called dead zones, such as the one in the Gulf of Mexico.

A long cylinder of ice drilled from a glacier or from the thick ice of Antarctica or Greenland. Bubbles of air trapped in the ice record past greenhouse gas levels going back hundreds of thousands of years.
The movement of people into a country (immigration) or out of it (emigration). Net migration is immigrants minus emigrants; it adds to or subtracts from the growth that births and deaths give.

A surface that water cannot soak through, such as pavement, roofs, parking lots and packed ground. Rain that falls on it runs off instead of infiltrating, so runoff and flooding increase and groundwater recharge falls.
Burning solid waste at high temperature. It reduces waste volume by about 90% and can generate electricity (waste-to-energy), but releases air pollutants and leaves ash that may be toxic.
A species whose presence, absence or health reveals the condition of its environment. Mayfly and stonefly larvae, for example, need clean, oxygen-rich water.
A pollutant in the air inside a building, such as radon, formaldehyde, carbon monoxide, asbestos fibers or smoke from indoor stoves. Tight, poorly ventilated buildings let them build up.

The number of babies who die before their first birthday, for every 1,000 babies born alive in a year. It is a key measure of a population’s health and is linked to fertility: where infant mortality is high, families tend to have more children.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can spread from one host to another, through water, air, food, contact or a vector.
The soaking of water from the land surface down into the soil and rock, which refills groundwater.
Infrared radiation (IR): invisible radiation with longer wavelengths than visible light, given off by warm objects such as Earth’s surface. Greenhouse gases absorb it.
Incoming solar radiation: the Sun's energy reaching an area, in watts per square meter (W/m²). It is greatest where sunlight strikes most directly, near the equator.

Integrated pest management (IPM): a way of controlling pests that combines monitoring with biological, physical, cultural and, only when needed, targeted chemical methods, to keep pests below the level that causes real economic damage while using as little pesticide as possible.
The property of an energy source that is not available all the time, such as solar at night or wind on calm days; it means storage or backup is needed.
The intertidal zone: the strip of shore covered by water at high tide and exposed to air at low tide, where organisms must resist drying and waves.
A nonnative (exotic) species, moved by people outside its native range, that spreads quickly and harms ecosystems, the economy or health. Many are generalists with r-selected traits.

The study of how many species live on islands and why. Larger islands and islands closer to a source of colonists hold more species. The ideas also apply to habitat islands such as lakes, mountaintops and forest fragments.

Describes species with a low biotic potential: few large offspring, much parental care, late first reproduction and long lives, such as elephants and whales. Their populations are fairly steady but recover slowly after losses.
The record of atmospheric carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii, since 1958 by Charles David Keeling and later NOAA. It rises every year with a small seasonal cycle.

A species whose effect on its community is much larger than its numbers suggest. Removing it changes the structure of the whole community, as when sea urchins multiply and strip kelp forests after sea otters disappear.
Units of energy: the joule (J), the kilowatt-hour (kWh, 3.6 million J), the British thermal unit (BTU, about 1,055 J) and the kilocalorie (kcal, about 4,184 J).
The cool phase of ENSO: the trade winds strengthen, upwelling off South America increases, the eastern Pacific is colder than average and rain is heavier in the western Pacific.
Ice on land: glaciers and the ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica. Its melt raises sea level. Sea ice, frozen seawater floating on the ocean, does not raise sea level when it melts.

Restoring land after mining: filling and regrading pits, replacing topsoil and planting native vegetation, so the land can support plants and wildlife again. In the United States a federal law requires coal mines to post money for it in advance.

The methane and CO2 produced when buried waste decomposes without oxygen. Landfills can capture it with wells and burn it to generate electricity (landfill gas to energy), a form of landfill mitigation.
Lethal dose 50%: the dose, in mg per kg of body mass, that kills half of a test population. A lower LD50 means a more toxic substance.
Liquid that forms when water seeps through buried waste and dissolves chemicals from it. Landfill liners and pipes collect it so it does not pollute groundwater.
The washing of dissolved substances, such as nitrate, down through the soil by water, toward underground water and streams.
A resource or condition that limits the growth of a population, such as food, water, space, nutrients, light, predators or disease.
The nutrient in shortest supply compared with what organisms need, so it limits growth; adding it increases growth. Nitrogen and phosphorus are common limiting nutrients.
The zones of a lake: the littoral zone (shallow edge with rooted plants), limnetic zone (open sunlit water), profundal zone (deep water too dark for photosynthesis) and benthic zone (the bottom).
A soil with a balanced mix of sand, silt and clay (roughly 40%, 40% and 20%). It drains well yet holds enough water and nutrients for most plants.
Growth that is fast at first, slows as resources run short, and levels off at the carrying capacity. It gives an S-shaped curve (S-curve), with the fastest growth at about half the carrying capacity.

Infectious diseases to know: malaria (protozoan, mosquitoes), tuberculosis (bacterium, airborne), cholera (bacterium, contaminated water), plague (bacterium, fleas), West Nile virus and Zika virus (mosquitoes), and SARS and MERS (respiratory viruses that passed from animals to people).
The idea, from the economist Thomas Malthus in 1798, that population tends to grow faster than the food supply, so it will be held back by famine, disease or war unless births fall.
A salt-tolerant tree that grows along tropical coasts and estuaries; mangrove forests hold sediment with their roots, protect shores from storms and shelter young fish.
The loss of a large share of Earth’s species in a geologically short time. Five have occurred; today’s rapid losses may mark a sixth mass extinction.

The largest amount of a resource that regrows, such as fish or timber, that can be harvested each year without reducing the population over time. For a population with logistic growth it is taken when the population is about half its carrying capacity, where it grows fastest.
Severe overheating of a reactor core after loss of cooling, so the fuel melts and radioactive material may escape, as at Three Mile Island, Chernobyl and Fukushima.

The mesosphere (about 50 to 85 km), where temperature falls with height to the coldest air in the atmosphere, and the thermosphere above it, very thin air heated sharply by the Sun. Its outer edge is the exosphere.
CH4, a gas made of one carbon and four hydrogen atoms, released by decomposition without oxygen (swamps, rice paddies, landfills), by cattle and from natural gas.

A toxic form of mercury made by bacteria in water and sediment from mercury released by sources such as coal burning and small-scale gold mining. It bioaccumulates and biomagnifies in fish and harms the developing nervous system.
A word part in front of a metric unit that multiplies it by a power of ten: kilo (10³), mega (10⁶), giga (10⁹), centi (10⁻²), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶).

Plastic pieces smaller than 5 millimeters, from larger plastic broken down by sunlight and waves, fibers from clothing, and small beads. Animals eat them, and they carry toxic chemicals into food webs.
Growing a single crop species, often a single variety, over a large area. It is efficient to plant and harvest but has low genetic diversity, so one pest or disease can spread through the whole crop.
The 1987 international treaty that phased out the production of CFCs, halons and other ozone-depleting substances; it has been ratified by every UN member state.
Municipal solid waste (MSW): everyday trash from homes, schools and businesses, such as paper, food, yard waste, plastics, metals and glass. It does not include industrial, mining or farm waste.
A relationship between two species in which both benefit (+/+), such as bees and the flowers they pollinate.

A natural event that changes an ecosystem, such as a flood, drought, wildfire, hurricane, volcanic eruption or a long-term change in climate. Disruptions can be periodic (regular), episodic (recurring at irregular intervals) or random (no pattern), and short-term or long-term. Also called a disturbance.
Pollutants released by natural processes rather than people: CO2 from volcanoes, wildfires, respiration and decomposition, and particles from volcanic ash, desert dust, sea spray, pollen and smoke.
A fossil fuel that is mostly methane; it releases about half as much carbon dioxide per unit of energy as coal, but it is not zero emissions.
The process by which individuals with heritable traits that suit their environment survive and reproduce more than others, so those traits become more common in the population over generations.
Net primary productivity: GPP minus the energy producers use for their own respiration (NPP = GPP - R). It is the energy stored as new plant matter and available to the animals that eat plants.
The role of a species in its ecosystem: what it eats, where and when it is active, and the conditions and resources it needs.
NO3−, the form of nitrogen made by nitrification that most plants take up. It dissolves easily and is not held by soil, so it leaches into water.
The conversion by soil bacteria of ammonium into nitrite and then nitrate, the form most plants take up.
The movement of nitrogen among the atmosphere, soil, water and living things through nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification.
The conversion of N2 gas from the air into ammonia or ammonium that living things can use, by bacteria (in soil and in legume root nodules), by lightning, or by industry making fertilizer.
NO and NO2, together written NOx. They form when nitrogen and oxygen in the air combine at the high temperatures of engines and power plants. NO2 is a brownish gas.

Nitrous oxide (N₂O): a greenhouse gas that traps roughly 265 to 300 times as much heat as the same mass of CO₂ over 100 years (the IPCC value depends on the report), released mostly by fertilized soils, manure and burning fuel. It lasts over a century in the air.

Planting seeds directly into the leftover residue of the last crop without plowing. The residue protects the soil, so erosion falls, more water soaks in, and soil organic matter builds up; weeds are usually controlled with herbicides or cover crops instead.

Sound at levels or times that harm people or wildlife, for example from traffic, aircraft, construction, industry or ships. It can damage hearing, raise stress and disrupt animal communication and migration.
Pollution that comes from many diffuse places rather than one outlet, such as runoff from farm fields, lawns and city streets, or exhaust from all the cars in a region.
A resource that exists in a fixed amount and forms far more slowly than people use it, such as coal, oil, natural gas and nuclear fuel.
The splitting of a heavy nucleus, such as uranium-235, when struck by a neutron, releasing a large amount of heat and more neutrons that can continue a chain reaction.
Radioactive material left from nuclear power, mainly spent fuel rods, which stays dangerous for thousands of years and must be stored away from people and water.
The decrease in the pH of seawater as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. Surface ocean pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since the 1700s.

A steady flow of ocean water, driven at the surface mainly by prevailing winds and turned by the Coriolis effect and the continents into large loops called gyres. Warm currents warm nearby coasts; cold currents cool them.
A release of petroleum into the environment, especially the ocean, from tankers, pipelines or drilling. Oil coats animals, destroying the insulation of feathers and fur, and poisons them.
The deep water of the ocean away from the coast. It covers most of Earth, but each square meter grows little algae because nutrients are scarce at the sunlit surface.
The part of a range of tolerance where individuals of a species grow, feed and reproduce best, so its population is largest.

Rock that contains enough of a valuable mineral, such as copper, iron, gold or lithium, to be mined at a profit. As the richest ores are used up, lower-grade ores must be mined, which moves more rock for each kilogram of metal.

Fertilizer from living things, such as manure, compost and plowed-in legumes. It releases nutrients slowly and adds organic matter that helps soil hold water and nutrients, but its nutrient content varies and is lower per kilogram than synthetic fertilizer.

The soil and rock that lie on top of an ore or coal deposit and are removed in surface mining. Tailings are the finely ground waste left after the valuable mineral is extracted from ore; both are piled near the mine and can release metals and acid.
Catching fish faster than the population can replace them by reproduction, so the stock shrinks year after year. It is a tragedy of the commons in the open ocean.
Grazing more animals on land than its plants can support, so plants are eaten faster than they regrow. Roots die, bare soil is exposed and compacted by hooves, and erosion follows.
The state of a population that has grown larger than the carrying capacity of its environment, so it uses resources faster than they are replaced.
A molecule of three oxygen atoms (O3). In the stratosphere it absorbs ultraviolet light; near the ground it is a pollutant that harms lungs and plants.
The thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer by chlorine and bromine from CFCs and halons. The ozone hole is the severe seasonal thinning over Antarctica each spring.
The region of the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 km up, where most of the atmosphere's ozone is found. It absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
A relationship in which a parasite lives on or in a host and feeds on it, benefiting while the host is harmed (+/−), usually without being killed right away.
The rock or sediment a soil forms from: the bedrock under it, or material carried in by rivers, glaciers or wind. It sets which minerals the soil starts with.
Tiny solid or liquid particles in the air, such as soot, dust and smoke. PM10 are 10 micrometers or smaller; PM2.5 are 2.5 micrometers or smaller and reach deepest into the lungs.
Heating and lighting a building with the sun through its design alone: sun-facing windows, overhangs and thick walls or floors that store heat, with no pumps or fans.
A living thing or virus that causes disease in its host: a bacterium, virus, protozoan, fungus or parasitic worm.
Partly decayed plant material from waterlogged bogs; the first stage in coal formation, with high moisture and low energy per kilogram.
Per person: a total divided by the number of people, used to compare places of different sizes.
A number out of 100. A share as a percent is the part divided by the whole, times 100; a percent of a quantity is (percent ÷ 100) times the quantity.
How much a value changed compared with its starting value: (new - old) / old × 100. Positive for an increase, negative for a decrease.
Soil that stays frozen all year. It lies under the tundra, keeps roots shallow and stores large amounts of dead plant matter.
How easily water flows through soil or rock. It depends on how large and well connected the pores are: high in sand, low in clay.

Pavement that lets water pass through it into a gravel layer and the soil below, through gaps between pavers or pores in the concrete or asphalt. It cuts runoff and recharges groundwater, but costs more and must be cleaned so its pores do not clog.
A persistent organic pollutant: a synthetic, carbon-based chemical that resists breakdown, dissolves in fat rather than water, travels long distances and is toxic. DDT, PCBs and dioxins are examples.

A substance used to kill or control organisms people consider pests. Insecticides kill insects, herbicides kill weeds, and fungicides kill fungi. Most act on many species, so they also harm nontarget organisms such as pollinators, predators of pests, and fish.

The ability of a pest population to survive a pesticide that once killed most of it. A few individuals carry genes that let them survive; spraying kills the others, the survivors breed, and over generations most of the population is resistant. It is natural selection caused by people.
Crude oil: a liquid fossil fuel formed from buried sea organisms and refined by boiling point into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, heating oil and asphalt.
A scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or basic a solution is: 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic, and each step is a tenfold change.
The form of phosphorus (PO4 with a negative charge) that plants take up and that makes up DNA, ATP, cell membranes, and bones and teeth. It clings to soil particles.
The movement of phosphorus among rock, soil, water, sediments and living things. It has no significant gas phase, so it is slow; weathering, uptake, decomposition and sedimentation move it.
The upper layer of a body of water where enough light reaches for photosynthesis. Below it lies the aphotic zone, which is too dark.

A brownish mix of secondary pollutants, mainly ground-level ozone, formed when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight. It is worst on hot, sunny afternoons in cities with heavy traffic.
The process in which plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing oxygen.
A photovoltaic (PV) cell turns sunlight directly into electricity, with no moving parts; many cells make a solar panel.

The first species to colonize a disrupted area: lichens and mosses on bare rock, or grasses and weeds on bare soil. They grow fast, spread easily and change conditions so that other species can follow.
The theory that Earth's rigid outer layer is broken into large plates that move slowly over the hotter mantle, driven by heat from inside Earth.
Pollution that enters the environment from one identifiable place, such as a factory discharge pipe, a sewage outfall, a smokestack or a leaking storage tank.
All the individuals of one species living in the same area at the same time.

A sharp drop in the size of a population, for example from hunting, a disease or a disaster. The few survivors carry only part of the original genetic diversity, so the population stays genetically less diverse even if its numbers recover.
The number of individuals of a population per unit of area or volume, such as 25 deer per square kilometer. Population density = number of individuals / area.

The tendency of a population with many young people to keep growing for decades even after families have fewer children, because the large young cohorts are still reaching the ages when people have children.
The share of a soil's volume that is pore space, the gaps between particles. Clay often has as much or more pore space than sand, but its pores are tiny.
A loop in which the result of a change strengthens that change, such as melting ice lowering albedo, which causes more warming and more melting.
A facility that makes electricity; in a thermal power plant, fuel heats water into steam that spins a turbine, which turns a generator.
Water that falls from the atmosphere as rain, snow, sleet or hail, usually measured in centimeters or millimeters.
An interaction in which one organism (the predator) kills and eats another (the prey). The predator benefits and the prey is harmed.

The four stages of the demographic transition. Preindustrial (1): high birth and death rates, slow growth. Transitional (2): falling death rate, high birth rate, fast growth. Industrial (3): falling birth rate, slowing growth. Postindustrial (4): low birth and death rates, little or no growth.

A fire set on purpose by forest managers under safe weather conditions to burn dead wood, fallen branches and brush on the forest floor. It removes the fuel that would let a wildfire grow large and hot, and helps species adapted to fire.
A pollutant released directly into the air by its source, such as carbon monoxide from a tailpipe or sulfur dioxide from a coal plant's smokestack.
The rate at which producers capture energy and build organic matter by photosynthesis in an area, such as kcal per square meter per year.

Succession that starts where there is no soil, such as new lava rock or rock exposed by a retreating glacier. Pioneer species such as lichens and mosses help form soil, so it is slow, often taking centuries.
The first, physical stage of sewage treatment: screens and grit chambers remove debris and sand, and settling tanks let solids sink as sludge while grease is skimmed off.
An organism that makes its own food from light (or chemicals) and simple substances, such as a plant, alga or photosynthetic bacterium; also called an autotroph.
The part of a fuel deposit that is known to exist and can be recovered profitably at current prices with current technology; it changes with prices, technology and production.
An ecosystem service that provides goods people take and use: food, fish, timber, fiber, fresh water and medicines.

Describes species with a high biotic potential: many small offspring, little or no parental care, early first reproduction and short lives, such as insects, mice and weeds. Their populations swing up and down and rebound quickly after disruptions.
The process in which an unstable nucleus gives off radiation and changes into a different element or isotope.
A colorless, odorless radioactive gas formed when uranium in rock and soil decays. It seeps into buildings through foundation cracks and is a leading cause of lung cancer.
A shallow, planted low spot that collects runoff from a roof, driveway or street and lets it soak into the ground. Deep-rooted plants and soil slow the water and trap sediment and some pollutants.
A dry region on the leeward side of a mountain range. Moist air drops its rain as it rises and cools on the windward side, then sinks and warms on the leeward side, bringing little precipitation.
The range of values of an abiotic factor, such as temperature or salinity, that an organism or population can survive. Also called ecological tolerance. Each species has a range for each factor.
A comparison of two quantities with different units, found by dividing, such as liters per day or people per square kilometer.
The growth of a population from births minus deaths, ignoring migration, as a percent per year: (crude birth rate minus crude death rate) divided by 10. It is negative when deaths outnumber births.
Collecting used materials such as aluminum, paper, glass and some plastics and processing them into new products. It saves resources and energy but costs money and energy to collect and sort.

Planting trees, or letting them regrow, on land where a forest was cut or burned. It restores habitat and carbon storage over decades; a plantation of one species restores far less biodiversity than a mixed native forest.
An ecosystem service that comes from natural processes keeping conditions stable for people: pollination of crops, purification of water, control of floods and erosion, and storage of carbon.
An energy source or resource that is replenished naturally at or near the rate people use it, such as sunlight, wind, moving water, Earth's internal heat and biomass.

The total fertility rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, about 2.1 children per woman where few children die young. It is above 2 because some children die before adulthood and slightly more boys than girls are born.
The way a species balances the number of offspring it produces against the care and resources given to each one. r-selected and K-selected are the two ends of the range of reproductive strategies.
A place where an element such as carbon is stored for a time, such as the atmosphere, the ocean, soil, living things or rock.
Species that compete for a resource dividing it by place, time or food size, which reduces competition so they can coexist.

Raising livestock on pasture, where the animals eat grass and other plants. In free-range grazing animals roam a large area; in rotational grazing the herd is moved from one fenced paddock to the next so grazed areas can regrow.
The rule of thumb that about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next; the rest is used for life processes and lost as heat.
A shortcut for doubling time: divide 70 by the percent growth rate. At 2% a year, 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years.
terms.topicTitle: Growth Rates, Doubling Time and the Rule of 70

terms.def: A hydroelectric system that runs part of a river's natural flow through turbines with little or no reservoir, so it floods little land but its output follows the river.
Water from rain or snowmelt that flows over the land surface into streams, rivers and lakes instead of soaking into the ground.
The amount of dissolved salt in water, often in parts per thousand (ppt). Freshwater is near 0 ppt and seawater about 35 ppt.

The buildup of salts in soil. Irrigation water carries small amounts of dissolved salt; when the water evaporates from the field, the salt is left behind, and over years it can reach levels that stunt or kill crops.
The movement of seawater into a coastal freshwater aquifer when fresh groundwater is pumped out faster than it is recharged. Wells near the coast begin to pump salty water.

An engineered site for burying solid waste, with a clay and plastic liner, leachate collection pipes, daily soil cover, methane gas wells and a final cap, designed to keep waste, liquid and gas from escaping.
A tropical grassland with scattered trees, warm all year, with a wet season and a long dry season; fires and grazing keep it open.
A way of writing a number as a number from 1 to 10 times a power of ten, such as 2.5 × 10⁶ for 2,500,000.
A device on a smokestack that removes sulfur dioxide (and some particles) from exhaust. A wet scrubber sprays a mixture of water and limestone; the SO2 reacts and is captured as a solid.
The rise in average ocean height, caused by melting land ice and by seawater expanding as it warms. Melting floating sea ice adds almost nothing.
A pollutant that forms in the air when primary pollutants react with each other, with oxygen, water or sunlight. Ozone near the ground and sulfuric acid are examples.

Succession that starts where soil remains after a disruption such as a fire, flood, hurricane or abandoned farm field. Because soil, seeds and roots remain, it is faster than primary succession, often taking decades.
The biological stage of sewage treatment: microbes in aerated tanks break down dissolved organic matter, greatly reducing its biochemical oxygen demand (BOD).
The settling of particles, such as shells and dead matter, to the bottom of water, where over long times they can harden into sedimentary rock such as limestone.

Harvesting only some of the trees in a forest, often single mature trees or small groups, and leaving the rest standing. It keeps forest cover, shade and habitat and limits erosion, but costs more per log than clearcutting.
A wastewater system for a single home: an underground tank where solids settle and bacteria break some down, and a drain field where soil filters the liquid that flows out.
The process of cleaning wastewater from homes and businesses before it is released, in stages: primary (physical), secondary (biological), tertiary (nutrient and chemical removal) and disinfection.
Sick building syndrome: headaches, eye irritation, coughing and tiredness that people feel in a particular building and that ease when they leave, usually from VOCs and poor ventilation.

A way of clearing land for farming by cutting the forest and burning what is left. The ash fertilizes the soil for a few seasons; when the nutrients run out the plot is left and a new one is cleared. It releases carbon dioxide and smoke and removes forest habitat.
The solid material removed from wastewater during treatment. It is usually digested by microbes (which can make methane for energy), then dried and landfilled, burned or used as fertilizer.
A soil's ability to supply the nutrients plants need. Clay and humus hold nutrients against leaching, and a pH near 6 to 7 keeps them available to roots.
One of the layers in a soil profile: O (organic matter), A (topsoil, humus mixed with minerals), B (subsoil, where leached minerals collect), C (partly weathered parent material), then bedrock.
The percentages of sand, silt and clay particles in a soil. The soil texture triangle turns the three percentages into a named texture class, such as loam or clay.
Reducing waste before it is created, for example by designing products with less packaging, making durable goods, or buying only what is needed. It is the most preferred step in the waste hierarchy.

A species with a narrow niche: it depends on a few foods, one kind of habitat or a narrow range of conditions, such as the giant panda and bamboo. Specialists are more likely to decline when their environment changes.
A group of similar organisms that can breed with one another and produce fertile offspring.
How equal the population sizes of the species in a community are. A community where each species has similar numbers is even; one dominated by a single species is uneven.
The number of different species in a community or area.

Irrigation that pumps water through pipes and sprays it over the crop like rain, as with a center-pivot sprinkler. It wastes less water than flood or furrow irrigation but costs more and uses energy for pumping; some spray evaporates or drifts in wind.
A rise in sea level pushed onto the coast by a storm's winds and low pressure. Mangroves, marshes and barrier islands reduce its height and force before it reaches homes.
terms.topicTitle: Human Impacts on Wetlands and Mangroves

terms.def: The layer above the troposphere, to about 50 km. It contains the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet light, so temperature rises with height.

Planting alternating strips of different crops, often a row crop such as corn beside a dense cover crop such as hay or clover, across a slope. The dense strips slow runoff and catch soil washed from the row-crop strips.

Mining deep deposits through vertical shafts and horizontal tunnels, leaving the surface mostly in place. It disturbs less land but is more expensive and more dangerous for miners (cave-ins, explosions, poor air) and can cause the ground above to sink.
SO2, a gas released mainly when coal and other sulfur-containing fuels burn. It irritates the airways and reacts in the air to form sulfuric acid.
An ecosystem service that the other services depend on: photosynthesis, nutrient cycling, soil formation and providing habitat.

Mining that removes the soil and rock above a deposit to reach ore or coal near the surface. It includes strip mining, open-pit mining and mountaintop removal. It is cheaper and safer for miners than subsurface mining but destroys habitat over large areas.

A graph of the number of individuals still alive at each age, out of a group born at the same time (often 1,000), usually with survivors on a log scale. Type I: most die old. Type II: a steady chance of dying at every age. Type III: most die young.

Using resources in a way that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs: resources that regrow, such as fish and forests, are used no faster than they regrow, and wastes are released no faster than the environment can absorb them.

Managing forests so that wood is harvested no faster than the forest regrows, while soil, water, habitat and biodiversity are protected for the future. It uses methods such as selective cutting, reforestation, protecting streamside trees, prescribed burns and reusing or recycling wood.
A close, long-term relationship between two different species: mutualism, commensalism or parasitism.
An interaction in which two or more substances together cause more harm than the sum of the harm each causes alone (a synergistic effect).

Fertilizer made in factories, mostly nitrogen (from ammonia made with natural gas), phosphorus and potassium in forms plants can take up at once. It raises yields quickly, but nutrients the crop does not use can run off or leach into water.
The boreal forest: a cold biome of cone-bearing evergreen trees with long, snowy winters and short summers, just south of the tundra.
Deposits of sand, clay, water and bitumen (a thick, heavy oil); the bitumen is mined or melted out with steam, using much energy and water, and upgraded to crude oil.
A temperate deciduous forest: a biome with warm summers, cold winters and rain through the year, whose broadleaf trees drop their leaves in fall.
A biome of grasses and few trees with hot summers, cold winters and moderate precipitation, such as a prairie. Its deep soils are very fertile for farming.
A coastal biome with mild temperatures and very heavy rain from ocean air, with huge conifers, mosses and ferns.
Cutting a steep slope into a series of flat steps (terraces) for growing crops. Each step holds water and soil, shortening the distance water can run downhill.
Extra treatment after the secondary stage that removes nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, and sometimes other chemicals, using filters and chemical or biological processes.
The increase in volume of water as it warms. Thermal expansion of seawater is one of the two main causes of sea level rise, with melting land ice.

A layer of warm air sitting above cooler air near the ground, the reverse of the normal pattern in which air cools with height. The cool, dense air cannot rise through the warm layer, so pollutants are trapped near the ground.
A harmful rise in the temperature of a body of water caused by people, mainly from power plant and factory cooling water and warm urban runoff. Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen.
A sudden change in water temperature that organisms cannot adjust to, such as when a plant starts or stops releasing warm water. It can kill fish and other aquatic life.
Thermohaline circulation (the ocean conveyor belt): the slow global movement of deep ocean water, driven by differences in temperature and salinity, which set the water’s density.
The highest dose at which no response is observed in a test population; on a dose-response curve, the point where the curve leaves zero.
Electricity made by turbines that catch the flow of ocean tides, which are caused by the moon's gravity, as they move in and out of a bay or channel.

Turning over and breaking up the soil with a plow or disk before planting, to bury weeds and crop leftovers and loosen the seedbed. It leaves the surface bare and loose, so it increases erosion by wind and water and speeds the loss of soil organic matter.
The average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime if birth patterns at each age stayed as they are now. Written TFR.
How harmful a substance is to living things. A toxicant is a substance that causes harm; the smaller the dose needed to cause harm, the higher the toxicity.

The steady surface winds of each latitude band: the trade winds (0° to 30°, from the east toward the equator), the westerlies (30° to 60°, from the west) and the polar easterlies (60° to 90°, from the east).

The overuse of a shared resource that no one owns or controls, such as an open pasture, an ocean fishery or an aquifer. Each user keeps the full benefit of taking more but shares the cost with everyone, so the resource is run down unless rules limit use.
A plate boundary where two plates slide past each other sideways. Stress builds and is released as earthquakes; there is little volcanic activity.
The release of water vapor from plants, mostly through small openings in their leaves. Evaporation and transpiration together are called evapotranspiration.
An organism’s position in a feeding sequence: producers are level 1, primary consumers level 2, secondary consumers level 3, tertiary consumers level 4.
A biome near the equator that is warm and very wet all year (often over 200 cm of rain), with dense, layered forest and soils poor in nutrients.
The lowest layer of the atmosphere, from the ground to about 10-16 km. It is heated from below, cools with height (about 6.5 °C per km), holds about 75% of the air's mass and nearly all weather.
A cold, treeless biome with long winters, a short growing season, little precipitation and permafrost, found at high latitudes and on high mountains.
Ultraviolet (UV) light: high-energy light from the Sun, shorter in wavelength than visible light. UV-B and UV-C damage DNA, causing skin cancer and cataracts and harming plants and plankton.
A rate for one unit of the second quantity, such as 150 liters per 1 person or 3 cm per 1 week.
The rise of cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface, often where winds push surface water away from a coast, as off Peru. It supports rich fisheries.
The radioactive metal used as nuclear fuel; reactor fuel is enriched to about 3 to 5 percent uranium-235, the isotope that splits easily.

A city that is warmer than the countryside around it, especially at night. Dark pavement and roofs absorb sunlight (low albedo), buildings and traffic release heat, and there are fewer plants to cool the air by transpiration.

The spread of low-density development, such as suburbs, shopping centers and roads, outward from a city onto farmland and natural land. It increases driving, paved area and cleared natural land per person compared with compact growth.
The growth of cities and the shift of a population from rural areas into urban areas. Over half of the world's people now live in cities.
A vapor recovery nozzle: a gas pump nozzle that captures gasoline vapor (VOCs) pushed out of a car's tank during refueling and returns it to the station's storage tank.
A volatile organic compound: a carbon-based chemical that evaporates easily, such as gasoline vapor, paint fumes and solvents. Trees also release some VOCs.
How much water a soil can hold after gravity drains the rest. It is highest in clay and soils rich in humus and lowest in sand.

Saturation of soil with water so that the pore spaces are full and roots cannot get the oxygen they need. Overirrigation and poor drainage cause it, and it can raise the water table toward the surface.

All the land that drains into one stream, river or lake, also called a drainage basin. High ground called a divide separates one watershed from the next. It is surface land, not underground water (an aquifer).
The watt (W) is a unit of power: one joule of energy per second. A kilowatt (kW) is 1,000 W and a megawatt (MW) 1,000,000 W. Energy = power × time.
The breakdown of rock into smaller pieces and dissolved minerals by water, ice, temperature changes, chemical reactions and living things. It releases phosphate and other nutrients into soil.
Land covered by shallow water or saturated with water for at least part of the year, such as a marsh or swamp. Wetlands store floodwater, filter pollutants and shelter wildlife.

Removing water from a wetland with ditches, pipes or fill so the land can be farmed or built on. It destroys wetland habitat and the services wetlands provide, such as flood storage and water filtering.
terms.topicTitle: Human Impacts on Wetlands and Mangroves

terms.def: A strip or link of habitat, such as a forested strip, an overpass or an underpass, that connects fragments so animals can move between them (also called a habitat corridor).
A machine whose blades are spun by the wind, turning a generator to make electricity; a group of them is a wind farm, on land or offshore.
A row of trees or shrubs planted along the edge of a field to slow the wind, reducing wind erosion and the drying of soil and crops. Windbreaks can also give habitat and wood.

The parts of a range of tolerance between the optimal range and the limits, where individuals survive but grow, feed or reproduce poorly. Beyond these zones lie the zones of intolerance, where individuals die.
